items.title: SNL Thread: Join us in watching Jalen Brunson host tonight!
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
After a week of preparation, NBA champion Jalen Brunson will walk the tightrope of hosting tonight. The newly crowned King of New York joins an elite club as one of the few NBA players ever to host the show, following Bill Russell, Charles Barkley, Michael Jordan, and LeBron James. The fact that this is the 52nd premiere of the iconic show makes the honor even more special, and while Jalen might not kill like OJ Simpson (hosted in ‘78), he can least land a joke better than that knucklehead Travis Kelce (’23). Tune in and watch along with us!

September 26, 2026 11:30 p.m. ET / 10:30 p.m. CT / 8:30 p.m. PT on NBC; streaming the next day on Peacock KATSEYE

Please don’t post large photos, GIFs, or links to illegal streams in the thread. Be good humans. And go Knicks!

items.title: Saturday Posted & Toasted Notes: KAT talks, falling stars, camp decisions, life choices
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Back-to-back daily Notes posts are all you need to know to start believing the season is right around the corner, starting with Monday’s media day. Can’t wait!

  • Karl-Anthony Towns’ contract situation remains the biggest storyline entering Knicks training camp. SNY’s Ian Begley reported the Knicks and Towns have remained in regular contact throughout the offseason, with discussions described as positive and the organization making clear it wants Towns in New York long term. However, no agreement is imminent.
  • Salary-cap expert Yossi Gozlan told Begley that extending Towns, Hart and McBride while also planning for future Jalen Brunson and OG Anunoby extensions will require difficult financial decisions unless the salary cap rises faster than projected or James Dolan changes his stance on going over the second apron.
  • ESPN’s Brian Windhorst and Tim MacMahon believe the two sides remain far apart financially, with the former saying there’s “tens of millions” separating them and MacMahon suggesting the gap could even be eight figures annually.
  • The Knicks’ final roster spot remains one of training camp’s biggest competitions, with Begley expecting veterans Bruce Brown, John Konchar and Ochai Agbaji to battle for a wing spot while Drew Eubanks and James Wiseman compete for the reserve center role. Unless New York sheds salary in a trade (looking at you, Paco), only of those five veterans is likely to make the standard roster.
  • Keeping it Begley, the pundit also expects rookie Tyler Nickel to receive one of the remaining camp spots and believes Kevin McCullar will eventually earn a place on the roster as well.
  • Jalen Brunson shared the defining moment that shaped his basketball career during an appearance on the “Things No One Tells You” podcast. His parents told him he could only choose two of three priorities: school, basketball, or a social life. You know what happened next.
  • Salty ESPN “analytics pioneer” Dean Oliver isn’t buying the consensus on Brunson’s standing among the league’s elite. While ESPN’s Top 100 panel ranked Brunson No. 6 overall, Oliver said his statistical models place the Finals MVP “around the No. 25 range” and argued New York media attention inflates public perception.

“I love Brunson’s game, but his lofty ranking benefitted not only from recent bias but also from the New York media bias. (That bias might also help you forget that Brunson missed the shot in the most iconic image from the Finals, when OG Anunoby swooped in for the putback game-winner to clinch Game 4.)

“The metrics place Brunson around the No. 25 range heading into the season. That’s not a huge gap. He’s elite, just not No. 6 — at least not during the regular season.”

  • Stephen Curry has agreed to a two-year, $116 million extension with the Warriors that includes a player option for the 2028-29 season. Curry, set to turn 39 midseason, still had one year left in his deal, meaning he could get to complete a nicely rounded 20-season career in The Bay if he retires at the end of his next pact.
  • Greg Oden admitted he never expected to be selected ahead of Kevin Durant in the 2007 NBA Draft and actually wanted to return to Ohio State.
  • North Macedonia great Pero Antić can only joke about making the Rising Stars Challenge at age 31. “I was already a falling star. Everyone was laughing, including my mom and dad.”

items.title: Friday Posted & Toasted Notes: KAT’s bag, Jordy McClarkson, salty RJ, married Pop
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
You know things are gearing up when you cook a fresh list of links and notes spanning just three days’ worth of news, and it already goes up to nearly 1K words. We’re so close to basketball, folks!

  • Jalen Brunson is hella ready. “I am…” he said, “fully cleared.” 
  • Karl-Anthony Towns’ extension talks with the Knicks have stalled with training camp approaching, and I have you covered here.
  • Don’t forget that, while the Towns negotiations take center stage, Josh Hart and Miles McBride remain extension-eligible too. McBride’s situation is particularly serious because he can become an unrestricted free agent next summer (Mitchell Robinson situation, anyone?), while Hart has a team option baked into his deal.
  • Jalen Brunson will officially make his Law & Order: SVU debut this fall. Brunson is scheduled to guest star in Season 28’s fifth episode on Nov. 5, reuniting him with Knicks superfan Mariska Hargitay after his recent Emmys cameo. His role remains under wraps.
  • In an interview with GQ Philippines, Jordan Clarkson discussed his up-and-down season with the Knicks, going from featured to end-of-the-bench fodder to postseason performer.

“I didn’t play for like a month, but me just being a pro, I had to stay locked in. I love this game, so I’m always ready. I stayed involved with the coaches, and with the young guys playing every day. My skill never wavered.

“The thing I learned being here this long is that everybody believes they’re the best player. They wouldn’t be here if they weren’t. So being able to put your ego to the side is important. It’s about coming together as a team, helping each other win without getting jealous, and having no ill intent towards any of your teammates.

“The whole season was a story on its own. Getting through adversity early in the playoffs, and not questioning ourselves. We had guys giving up a lot for this.”

  • Clarkson also wants another run with the Philippines at next year’s FIBA World Cup.

“Another World Cup is coming up, and I want to be there. There haven’t been so many Filipino Americans in the [NBA] league, and Filipinos, period. So knowing that I get to represent that and kind of change the narrative in any way that I can, that’s what I’m trying to do. Hopefully, we can see those dudes [Jalen Green and Dylan Harper] in a Gilas jersey at some point.”

  • Mitchell Robinson had strong praising words for Jalen Brunson’s leadership after leaving the Knicks for Boston, saying “Jalen is so dialed in.”
  • The Knicks have hired Ed Flynn as Mike Brown’s new replay and challenge specialist. Flynn spent the previous three seasons as a video coordinator with the Pelicans and replaces Jordan Brink.
  • The final Knicks roster spot remains a genuine training-camp competition between James Wiseman, Drew Eubanks, Bruce Brown, John Konchar and Ochai Agbaji. The NYP’s Stefan Bondy outlined one possible wrinkle to that roster battle: moving Pacome Dadiet could allow the Knicks to retain two camp invitees instead of one. A larger trade remains another possibility if neither Wiseman nor Eubanks convinces the Knicks they have enough at center, with Bondy identifying Miles McBride as New York’s most valuable expendable trade piece. Go read it all!
  • The Ringer placed the defending champion Knicks second in its preseason NBA power rankings, behind only San Antonio and ahead of Oklahoma City.
  • The Knicks have a relatively favorable travel calendar overall, with only 13 back-to-backs and roughly 35,181 road miles, the second-fewest in the NBA.
  • New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is not interested in paying championship-inflated MSG prices to attend Opening Night at MSG. “Brother, I do not have $2,000 ready for that ticket.”
  • OAKAAK RJ Barrett admitted there was a little bitterness watching his former team win the championship, but ultimately was happy for his old teammates.

“At first, definitely feel a little salty, but if anybody else were to win it, I’m happy they won it. I still have friends over there.” He added that he hopes to bring some of that success to Toronto.

  • Jalen Duren and Detroit continue to have one of the stranger contract negotiations of the offseason, with the Pistons offering him a five-year, $200 million offer… that includes weight-based incentives requiring Duren to check his weight monthly.
  • Steven Adams believes Grand Theft Auto VI could tank pro sports.
  • OAKAAK Kevin Knox is getting another NBA opportunity, signing an Exhibit 10 deal with Orlando for training camp.
  • NBA expansion is getting closer, with Las Vegas appearing further along than Seattle. The league has already held multiple bidding deadlines for Las Vegas and could reportedly identify a winning group there before settling on its Seattle plans.
  • Shaquille O’Neal makes around $15 million annually in sports media, Charles Barkley about $21 million, Pat McAfee roughly $30 million, and Tom Brady $37.5 million. Stephen A. Smith tops the list reported by The New York Post, at around $40 million per year across his media deals. Sheesh…
  • Gregg Popovich married Mary Barth Budenholzer, the former wife of longtime Spurs assistant Mike Budenholzer, on Sept. 16 in Texas.

items.title: Can the Knicks afford to play hardball with Karl-Anthony Towns?
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
Ah, training camp. Finally back into the swing of things with basketball. It really is a lot more peaceful as defending champions, isn’t it?

Let’s see what’s going on as Media Day nea-

Ah, I guess we were overdue for negative.

Karl-Anthony Towns is eligible for a contract extension this offseason. It’s been assumed, especially after a championship, that Towns and the Knicks were going to be tied at the hip going forward, but the complicated mechanisms of the salary cap and second apron will of course serve as a boogeyman for roster building.

Now, what Shams has reported seems to be a bit dramatic based on what several Knicks reporters have said about the situation, but the consensus seems to be that the two sides are not nearing any sort of agreement as of yet.

As we know, Towns is eligible for a four-year, $276 million extension, but he will not receive that figure. It’s nothing personal, he could absolutely argue he’s worth it considering guys like De’Aaron Fox and Trae Young make north of $200 million, it’s just not practical for roster construction.

With James Dolan seemingly adamant about not exceeding the second apron, this negotiation will be walking a tightrope. The Knicks undoubtedly want to chop down the $61 million that Towns is currently due on a player option in 2026-27 because that figure would make things extremely awkward next offseason.

By current projections, the Knicks have $221.3 million on the books in 2027-28 if we assume KAT opts into his player option, they pick up Josh Hart and Tyler Kolek’s team options, and decline Pacome Dadiet’s. That would put the team $12.5 million beneath the second apron with five mandatory roster spots to fill. There is a way to do that; it would just ensure that Deuce McBride walks, and the team can’t use anything other than a vet min.

Cutting that number to, say, $50 million (Ian Begley suggests that’s on the table) for a new extension would give them $23.5 million in space beneath the apron, giving the team significantly more flexibility. Anything lower? They’d feasibly be able to give McBride a market-value extension.

So you can see what the vision is for Leon Rose and company to keep this contention window open, but Towns is going to have to play ball.

From his vantage point, why should he play ball? He’s an NBA champion, was arguably the most important piece of the team’s 13-game playoff winning streak, and played exceptional defense on Victor Wembanyama. Why should he have to be cut the same checks as Trae Young and De’Aaron Fox, two guys who’ve shown they can’t be winning players?

Jalen Brunson taking his pay cut may have opened an organizational Pandora’s Box, expecting everyone to take less, but it has nothing to do with him or the team, it has everything to do with the aprons.

It’s simple. The only way to have a sustainable winner in this CBA is to have a plethora of draft capital and high draft picks, or have guys take pay cuts. Option 1 closed as soon as Brunson got to New York and ended any potential tank talk, so there’s only one option.

If the two sides can’t hash anything out by October, it’s not the end of the world. They can agree to terms at any time; there’s no deadline like there is for rookie-scale extensions, but you get concerned because in-season extensions for All-Stars are rare. If we get to Opening Night with no deal, this might just bleed into next summer, something that you want to avoid.

Next summer, Towns has a player option. Now, many times when a player has the option to opt into a huge salary like that, they take it, but there’s a chance he doesn’t. After all, he could sign a deal of up to $264 million across four years in free agency next summer with someone else, or could even get as much as a baffling five-year, $357.3 million supermax in a sign-and-trade or extremely late extension. That’s a lot of cash, all of which the Knicks can’t feasibly match.

The risk that you take is that a team with cap space next offseason can just try to scoop up Towns next offseason, but how much of a risk is that? After all, stars rarely change teams in free agency anymore. Who even has cap space?

That’s more teams with room than usual, but $50 million gets you a lot less than it used to. As of right now, only the Nets have true max salary space, with the Bulls and Clippers close behind. None of those teams are competitive, so signing there indicates you just want a bag and don’t want to win. I know KAT loves New York, but I don’t think he loves Brooklyn much.

Obviously, a sign-and-trade would be the most likely thing to happen if the relationship deteriorates that much, but things just shouldn’t go there. A big reason why this Knicks team succeeded was because of the good vibes that persisted in a team that always believed in each other. Ego is the downfall of every good team, and the Knicks can’t afford that.

That’s the bigger risk of letting this bleed out than the risk of losing Towns. I’d be utterly stunned if an extension wasn’t eventually agreed to, whether today, tomorrow, or in June 2027, both sides need it.

Towns deserves to be a Knick for the rest of his career and see his No. 32 lifted into the rafters, but the two sides are going to have to find a middle ground. There are non-negotiables here, both with Towns getting a max and the Knicks getting him to take a ridiculous pay cut.

The staring contest will continue, but someone has to blink. Neither side can afford eye drops.

items.title: Karl-Anthony Towns extension talks stall as Knicks face $276 million question
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Karl-Anthony Towns and the New York Knicks are approaching training camp without a contract extension, and one of the biggest financial questions surrounding their championship core remains widely unresolved.

ESPN’s Shams Charania and Vincent Goodwill first reported Wednesday that extension talks have stagnated following extensive offseason discussions. An agreement is considered unlikely before training camp, with media day scheduled for Monday.

“Talks have been described to me as cordial, there just has not been movement on a deal — especially as of late,” Charania reported.

Towns is eligible for an extension worth up to four years and $276 million, according to ESPN’s Bobby Marks. He will earn $57 million this season and holds a $61 million player option for 2027-28.

Newsday’s Steve Popper confirmed that the Knicks and Towns remain far enough apart that negotiations could linger into the regular season and potentially beyond.

New York has made it clear that the franchise wants to keep Towns, and league sources have indicated Towns is willing to accept less than his maximum contract to re-sign with the Knicks.

The central disagreement appears to be how large that discount will be. New York is attempting to preserve flexibility while owner James Dolan has publicly pushed to keep the franchise below the punitive second apron, but there might be a breaking point Towns is not willing to get past.

Even then, SNY’s Ian Begley reported that conversations have remained positive and that the Knicks have made clear they want Towns long-term. Begley also revealed that New York has discussed extension structures with Towns beginning in the $45 million-to-$50 million annual range.

Those figures would leave Towns well below his maximum, yet The New York Post’s Stefan Bondy also emphasized that neither side has abandoned an agreement even though talks have stalled a bit.

“There’s been plenty of conversations with KAT, all cordial, all positive,” Bondy reported, citing a league source. “(Knicks) want KAT to be (there) for a long time. And just because a deal isn’t done now doesn’t mean it can’t get done.”

Towns, meanwhile, publicly expressed the same desire to stay in New York last winter. “Hell yeah I want to stay here,” Towns told The New York Post in December. “Obviously, get a chance to be home, see my family. It means more than the money, you know. So just to be able to be here with the fans, be with the family. It means a lot. I would like it to continue.”

ESPN’s Brian Windhorst identified Towns’ $61 million option and the Knicks’ self-imposed second apron restriction as the heart of the negotiations and the main hurdle to clear before an agreement is reached.

“What KAT does will determine if Knicks core can stay together,” Windhorst said. “He’s got a $61 million option for not this season, next season. Knicks have said, ‘We don’t wanna be in second apron.’ If he picks up that option, they’re gonna be in the second apron.”

Windhorst believes the relationship between Towns’ agency, CAA, and the Knicks increases the chances of a deal. Knicks president Leon Rose previously represented Towns, while CAA also represents Jalen Brunson and other New York players.

“I honestly believe this is all gonna work out even if, again, you hear a little bit of wavering in the first couple of days of camp,” Windhorst said. “If James Dolan messes this up. Let Leon Rose and CAA do their business, and I think Karl-Anthony Towns will figure it out.”

The Knicks already allowed Mitchell Robinson to leave in free agency while managing their second-apron restriction. Josh Hart is also extension-eligible, while Brunson and OG Anunoby will become eligible next offseason, making for a tight cap situation in New York.

For now, Towns will report to training camp without a new agreement but ready to help the Knicks defend the title it took the franchise 53 years to reclaim.

items.title: Tyler Nickel’s Knicks future takes shape ahead of training camp
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The New York Knicks have yet to sign rookie Tyler Nickel, but the expectation around the league is that the two sides will ultimately reach an agreement.

Nickel joined the Knicks organization after New York used the No. 47 overall pick on the former Vanderbilt standout, but there were questions about whether or not the sharpshooter would eventually join the NBA roster.

On Wednesday, The Athletic’s James L. Edwards III reported that while Nickel’s status remains unresolved ahead of training camp, it’s likely he ends up sitting on the Knicks’ bench and getting minutes this season after eventually inking a deal in the next few days or weeks.

“From everything I’ve heard from talking to people throughout the league, Nickel and the Knicks are expected to reach some kind of contract agreement,” Edwards wrote.

What kind of contract Nickel receives, however, is less certain. Edwards noted that Nickel could make more through NIL by returning to college than on a two-way contract with New York, with early-summer reports of a possible $1-to-$1.4 million NIL deal waiting for him if he returns. A federal court ruling granted Nickel and a few other young men a fifth year of eligibility, so that door is wide open.

The situation could potentially explain New York’s roster construction to date, with open spots and a bunch of players in tryout deals heading into preseason. All we know is that New York is expected to add one more player on a standard contract before the season while surely avoiding the second apron.

“Could the Knicks be trying to make a trade to open up a roster spot to give Nickel a standard deal?” Edwards wrote. “The way this situation has played out, it sort of feels that way.”

Edwards identified Pacôme Dadiet and Miles McBride as logical trade possibilities if New York chooses that route, although he is skeptical McBride would be moved before the season.

While Nickel remains unsigned, Edwards’ reporting makes it very clear the expectation is that the Knicks and their second-round pick eventually reach an agreement. For now, we wait.

items.title: Thirty-Third and Thriving
items.author: John Gove
items.content:
Let us rewind for a moment.

It is June 18, 2026. The New York Knicks are finally NBA Champions, parading through the Canyon of Heroes amongst an expansive sea of orange-and-blue faithful. Jalen Brunson takes the microphone, holding the Larry O’Brien Trophy over his head, ready to address a fanbase that has waited for this moment since 1973. When he speaks, he rightfully takes the time to acknowledge his teammates and thank his coaches. But he doesn’t stop there. He also takes time to address the people he’s used as motivation for as long as he can remember—the haters.

Of course, some may view this as holding a grudge. But this isn’t the Michael Jordan Hall of Fame speech 2.0. These words don’t reflect pettiness on Brunson’s part. Instead, it highlights the true foundation of his success. His quiet and relentless edge and determination to silence doubters made him the reigning king of New York and a poster child for underdogs everywhere.

As summer comes to an end and training camp draws near, the traits that led Brunson to an NBA Championship also shine through in a different avenue. His family officially launched a management group. It is a new advisory firm dedicated to supporting athletes, executives, and NIL talent.

What’s the name of this firm? Well, it’s Thirty-Third.

On thirty-two separate occasions during the 2018 NBA Draft, front offices looked at the resume of one of the most decorated amateur basketball players. They said, “no thanks,” and went in a different direction. It took until the 33rd pick for Dallas to call his name and make him a Maverick. When you look at his pre-draft bragging list, it’s hard to fathom how a player with that much success could fall to the second round.

Let’s have a read through his accomplishments. I bet you can’t get through it without your eyes watering up and forcing you to blink (thanks for that one, Russell Richardson).

In 2014, he won gold with FIBA Americas at 18. A year later, he was an Illinois Class 4A Champion, the state’s Mr. Basketball, a McDonald’s All-American, and the USA Basketball Male Athlete of the Year. Then, he went to the FIBA Under-19 World Cup, won gold, made the All-Tournament Team, and took home MVP. That was all before he arrived at Villanova.

As a freshman Wildcat, he won a national championship. By his junior year, he didn’t win another title; he brought home all the glory. He was the consensus National College Player of the Year. He took home both the Wooden and Naismith Awards. He won the Bob Cousy Award as the nation’s top point guard. He earned AP, USBWA, NABC, and Sporting News Player of the Year honors. He was a first-team All-American and the Big East Scholar-Athlete of the Year.

Today, his jersey hangs in Villanova’s rafters, providing him a place among collegiate immortality.

Still, NBA talent evaluators scoffed at the idea that Brunson would amount to anything notable after college. Even with all the evidence to the contrary, 32 other names that did not rhyme with “Falen Dunson” came through the speakers. They paid closer attention to his height, or lack thereof, than to his footwork. They focused on his vertical instead of his efficiency. Others’ misfortunes translated into a draft steal for the Mavericks.

Crazily enough, they ended up underestimating him too.

The draft-night disrespect was only the opening scene of a story flooded with underappreciation and nonsensical criticism. The haters followed him to Dallas, where the Mavericks brass showed their incompetent roster-management skills more than once. We’re not even talking about Luka here!

After landing the steal of the century, the Mavs never truly recognized Brunson’s value. Eligible for a contract extension before the 2021-22 season, Brunson’s team put a four-year, $55 million deal on the table. Given the financial climate, this was a huge bargain for Dallas and a no-brainer. Unfortunately, the Mav brass looked the old gift horse in the mouth (or whatever that saying is) and hesitated. They prefer the reliable “wait-and-see approach,” claiming they needed to evaluate a sample size before committing that much green.

Then Luka got hurt, allowing Brunson to step into the primary role, where he brilliantly orchestrated the offense. Even with all the chips on their side of the table, Brunson’s camp went back to the front office and said they were still willing to commit to the prior deal. Unfortunately, it takes two to tango, and Dallas wasn’t in the mood to dance.

By the time the Mavs realized they needed to pay the man, the price went up, and the relationship was rockier than the Shipwreck Coast in Australia. Look it up; it’s real rocky.

Of course, one team’s failure is another one’s success. Dallas’s fumbling of the Brunson situation led to good old Uncle Leon swooping in and bringing him to the Knicks on a four-year, $104 million contract.

Surprisingly (not), the media pooped all over that decision.

The reaction to the signing was incredibly negative. Critics laughed at the Knicks for committing that kind of money to a “role player.” Bleacher Report even went so far as to grade the acquisition a C. To many “experts,” the Knicks overpaid for a secondary piece who made his name by riding Luka’s coattails.

Even as Brunson immediately changed the culture of a cursed franchise, new avenues for doubt emerged. He led New York to the playoffs, earned an All-Star spot, made the All-NBA Second Team, and became the Garden’s go-to guy. Still, the chuckleheads behind desks and cameras would not retreat. Becky Hammon even went on national television and told the world that even though Brunson was a phenomenal talent, a team couldn’t win with a 6-foot-2 guard as their “1A.”

He faced the same skepticism on draft night. This time, the audience was bigger… by a lot. None of it was about his production. Instead, it was about old rules chiseled in stone: “short” dudes can’t lead a team to the promised land.

Of course, Brunson went and smashed that old stone to bits.

He won NBA Clutch Player of the Year. He led the team to the NBA Cup and won the tournament MVP. Then, in a postseason where everybody could find reasons the Sixers, Cavs, and Spurs would beat the Knicks, Brunson went and won a flippin’ championship.

At 30, “Captain Clutch” keeps silencing doubters. He proved Dallas wrong. He proved 32 teams that passed on him wrong. He even forced the media to eat their previous statements and admit that he was indeed a 1A superstar.

A complete masterstroke, starting Thirty-Third is the ultimate “nanny-nanny” to everyone who attached the word “nope” to his name. By focusing on athletes, executives, and underserved markets like women’s professional sports, Brunson and his family are building something to help others avoid the same challenges he was forced to navigate. They are ensuring talent and production drive value, not preconceived notions and archaic scouting philosophies.

Undervalued at every single turn of his basketball life, Brunson never altered his game or mindset. He took on the disrespect and burned the pillars of unjustified criticism to the ground. Once the thirty-third pick, he is now a champion, finally silencing the haters who fueled his flame.

items.title: The unique brilliance of Jalen Brunson
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
In the immediate aftermath of winning a championship, there’s utter jubilation. Once that initial high wears off after the ceremony and you start truly grasping what you just witnessed, the human mind naturally goes in a completely different direction.

You begin to think of those who were proven wrong.

Athletes always say after they win it all, “They didn’t believe in us,” or “What’re they gonna say now?” They feed off slander. Any time in life that you or something you care about gets disrespected, you long for the day that person has to eat crow and face the music. It’s just human nature.

For the basketball world, after the final buzzer sounded on June 13, that vitriol was directed towards one person.

After a few months to really ponder things, my tone has shifted toward Becky, even if only slightly.

In that clip, Hammon expresses her opinion, which is based on the last 35 years of NBA basketball. Only one team has won a championship with a small guard as their best player since the Bad Boys Pistons from 1989-90, and even then there’s an exception because almost all of their identity came from smashmouth defense that had nothing to do with I.T.

You can’t win if your best player is small. The one exception was Steph Curry, who changed the game of basketball forever with the 3-point revolution. Unless you have a generational talent, an outlier with impact so drastic that you have to provide additional context for his cultural impact, your best player cannot be a small guard if you want to win a championship.

She was right about her overall premise. She was just wrong about the one person she singled out.

There are loads of small guards that Becky could’ve singled out. Ja Morant, Donovan Mitchell, Damian Lillard, Kyrie Irving, prime Russell Westbrook, Trae Young, De’Aaron Fox, etc. All of these guys were No. 1 options at or before the time of her remarks in December 2023. She has never, on record, talked about any of them as guys who can’t win.

Her problem was that she singled out Jalen Brunson. The odds were in her favor that she would never have to answer for her misdeeds, but her desire to ride the “Knicks for Clicks” wave was her undoing. Of all the typical, ball-dominant, non-winners in the world she could’ve ragged on, she decided to choose the only one who would ever be able to prove her wrong.

What Brunson did isn’t a blueprint. It isn’t a fluke. It wasn’t asterisk-worthy. It was a definitive statement that he belongs in the same conversation as Curry as an outlier, as a player who stands amongst giants and doesn’t back down, as a player whose playstyle allows him to overcome the true reality of smaller guards being at a disadvantage in the modern NBA.

For the last few years, we’ve heard the same phrase, “Who’ll be the next Jalen Brunson?” The answer is nobody will be, because if it were that easy to be Jalen Brunson, it wouldn’t be as utterly shocking to the NBA landscape as his lifting the Larry O’Brien Trophy turned out to be.

It’s a story that honestly goes a helluva lot deeper than even I can chronicle.

They say that the son of a role player is more likely to be the star than the son of a superstar, and that personifies the Brunson’s to a T. Role players know what held them back from stardom and can pass down to their sons what it means to not always be the best player on the court.

We saw the countless stories of Rick Brunson having a young Jalen work hard to master his craft, not take shortcuts, and do everything he can to overcome not always being blessed with the genetic makeup of a can’t-miss superstar.

You see it all throughout his career: how he had to constantly prove people wrong to get to the next level. He had to continue to work and change his game to prevent stagnation. He never accepted being shoehorned into a role. His work ethic is 1-of-1 and something that defines his path to where he is today.

The best example I can find of him evolving his own game to help him reach the next level is his floater evolution. Did you know that, back at Villanova, Brunson never shot floaters? Something that he’s currently the best at in basketball used to be totally alien to him.

Why did a young Brunson, who was still shorter than everyone else and should’ve had this in his toolbag as soon as possible, not attempt many? It was apparently a Villanova edict. Jay Wright did not want his guards to attempt floaters. For six consecutive years, the perennially contending Wildcats were dead last in floater attempts, something that was personal for Wright.

He wanted his players to finish off two feet. It was drilled into them in every practice from the moment they stepped on campus.

Watching Brunson’s college highlights, you can see the footwork that makes him who he is today. It reminds us that it usually takes a village to raise a warrior, as Brunson learned his impeccable footwork by developing in an incredible system for multiple years, while later adding the floater to take advantage of time and space. He was able to do both once he was given the freedom to.

When he did start attempting more floaters towards the end of his tenure in Dallas, you saw flashes of what he would become in New York. He was just hidden in a system that revolved around Luka Doncic. You saw what he could be when he was out, especially against the Jazz in the 2022 playoffs.

It was really a perfect storm when he came to New York. He got to return to a place he cared so deeply about, playing for the father who pushed him to be great, in a support system with many lifelong friends and family around the team; he got the ability to be ball-dominant, and he got to unleash the love child of the footwork he meticulously developed in college and the elite touch and jumper he got from grinding for more playing time in Dallas, all while doing the one thing he has done his whole life: prove everyone wrong.

Maybe we should’ve seen this all coming.

There’s also one aspect that I’ve neglected to mention that has nothing to do with his basketball ability, which he has in spades.

There’s an old-school form of leadership that Brunson possesses, one that you don’t see almost anywhere else that doesn’t have a grizzled, Udonis Haslem-esque veteran. Despite never winning an NBA championship or even coming close, he carried himself like one.

A perk of growing up as the son of an NBA player is that you will learn what to do and what not to do. Rick was certainly not infallible, and the mistakes he made growing up shaped Jalen into the non-problematic star he is today.

You look around the league, and you see divas. You see people who clap back on Twitter burners when they’re being slandered; you see people take thinly veiled shots at teammates through the media; you see players be hostile towards fans and the press; you see them get in trouble with the law in one of a million different ways. Distractions, controversy, and immaturity. All of that can consume you, especially in a media market like New York.

That doesn’t happen with the Knicks, and it starts with their captain and leader. They got to this point by playing like a team of brothers who all have each other’s backs, and it’s how they’ve managed to pick each other up after every early deficit and punch in the mouth they receive. No matter how bad it gets, they don’t point fingers.

It’s why I cannot stand people saying, “Well, if *insert point guard* had a supporting cast like that, they’d win too,” Kyrie Irving is someone who’s been used as a point of comparison with Brunson all season, with heated debates ongoing about who’s better.

It’s Brunson. Full stop. Irving was embarrassing every time he had to lead a team.

Don’t give me the crap that he didn’t get to lead a team like Brunson’s. Sure, the Baby Jays from 2017-19 weren’t an ideal situation, but it was one he could’ve embraced and turned into something beautiful if he gave it time. Hell, they were an ECF-caliber team despite Gordon Hayward’s leg being sideways and two of their starters not being old enough to drink. Instead, he was a diva and gave up on trying to be “the guy,” and settled for being a sidekick to KD and eventually James Harden in Brooklyn.

So to sum this all up, here’s something to leave you with.

Becky Hammon was right. Small guards almost never win titles as the top option. You do need a “1A dude”.

But she picked the wrong guy to single out, because history will remember Brunson as the exception to the rule, one that defied every odd and left the NBA world wondering how he did it.

items.title: Mike Brown has a new set of eyes on the iPad
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
You and a buddy are watching the Knicks game at home when the refs make an egregiously erroneous call. The two of you hurl obscenities and whatever’s handy at the TV. Meanwhile, on the sideline, coach Mike Brown flaps his arms as if trying to fly, but he’s unsure of whether to call a challenge. He cranes his neck toward someone in the second row behind his bench. Your buddy asks, “Who’s the dork with the iPad?”

In Game 2 of the Finals, the eagle eyes of assistant coach Jordan Brink led to a challenge that became three OG Anunoby free throws with 2:37 remaining in the Knicks’ 105-104 victory over San Antonio. One assistant coach watching an iPad helped alter an NBA Finals game. I didn’t spot Brink at the victory parade—frankly, I couldn’t pick him out of a lineup—but he deserved a prominent spot among the celebration. 

Brink’s official title was a lot to fit on a business card: Assistant Coach / Director of Video Services and Player Development. Unfortunately, his contract expired after last season, and he accepted an assistant-coaching position on Tiago Splitter’s Chicago staff. Seems like a nice promotion. 

According to Stefan Bondy of the , the Knicks have hired Ed Flynn to fill the job. He was formerly the head video coordinator for New Orleans. Like Brink, Flynn will serve as Brown’s primary “challenge guy,” monitoring replay and advising Brown in real time on whether to challenge officials’ calls.

Before his three seasons with the Pelicans organization, he did video work with Charlotte and a graduate-assistant stint at Miami.

Don’t sleep on these video guys. Many prominent NBA head coaches and assistants began their careers chewing up film in dark backrooms as video coordinators or video interns. Spoelstra, Vogel, Malone, Budenholzer, Clifford all spring to mind. And even Mike Brown started as an unpaid video intern with the Nuggets.

One day you’re eating stale pizza way past midnight to get a series of clips ready for the coach in the morning. A few years later, you’re getting showered with confetti in the Canyon of Heroes.

After the addition of Flynn, the Knicks’ primary assistants otherwise remain intact: Chris Jent, Rick Brunson, Brendan O’Connor, Maurice Cheeks, and Darren Erman are returning, as are development coaches Kwadzo Ahelegbe and Peter Patton.

Welcome Ed! You’ll never be just a dork with an iPad to us.

items.title: Wiseman may have an edge in the Knicks’ five-man roster battle
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Today, Marc Stein reported that New York expects to carry 14 standard contracts rather than 15. That means the five veterans brought to camp (Bruce Brown, John Konchar, Ochai Agbaji, Drew Eubanks, and James Wiseman) are effectively duking it out for one job unless the Knicks clear some cash.

From the latest :

“It’s believed that the Knicks will only fill one of the two current vacancies in terms of the maximum 15 standard contracts they can carry starting Opening Night (Oct. 21) unless they make another roster move first that sheds salary.”

At present, New York sits only a little more than $3 million below the second apron, leaving enough room for one additional veteran-minimum contract but not two. With the Knicks needing more help at center than on the wing, it sure seems that Eubanks and Wiseman are frontrunners for the open gig.

But wait! There’s another wrinkle. Stein also reports:

“Brown, furthermore, is indeed a Wiseman fan. The newly crowned champs likewise do appear to have a clear need for a third big man behind Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond.”

You’ll recall that Brown was an assistant coach for the Warriors when they selected Wiseman second in the 2020 draft. He must’ve helped to evaluate the young player out of Memphis, and perhaps he spotted potential that hasn’t yet been realized on the NBA court. The 6’11”, 240lb big man averaged 11.5 points and 5.8 rebounds in 21.4 minutes across 39 games (27 starts) as a rookie, but his year was cut short by a torn right meniscus. After that, the injury bug continued to chase him through Detroit and Indiana.

“James—he does stuff on a daily basis that makes you sit back and go, ‘Wow. Did he just do that? Am I seeing that?’ The sky is the limit for him. I don’t know if there’s anything that he’s not gonna be able to do when he reaches his peak.”

If Wiseman lives up to that high praise in New York’s training camp, his former coach is very likely to lock him down for the opening night roster. Meanwhile, while searching for a cover picture, your humble blogger found a few too many images of Mitchell Robinson dunking on Wiseman. Which stung.
